title: I have a headache — the body and its complaints
title_target: मेरे सिर में दर्द है — mere sir meⁿ dard hai
goal: Explain how you feel to a doctor or pharmacist — with a sentence pattern that, once again, doesn't make "I" the owner of the pain but the place where it happens.

dialogs.title: संवाद — At the doctor's
dialogs.intro: Ani falls ill after two days of trying street food. This conversation is full of words Hindi borrowed from Arabic and Persian — some of which have shifted in meaning, and the notes on the next page show which.

lines.speaker: डॉक्टर:
lines.id: Please, what seems to be the trouble?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: I have a headache, and a fever too.
lines.literal: my — head — in — pain — is, and — fever — also — is.

lines.speaker: डॉक्टर:
lines.id: Is your stomach all right? Did you eat something outside?
lines.literal: stomach — fine — is? something — outside — of — eaten?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, yesterday I ate something by the roadside.
lines.literal: yes, yesterday — road — on — something — eaten — was.

lines.speaker: डॉक्टर:
lines.id: (smiling) I see. First time in India?
lines.literal: (smiling — while) understood — did(masc.). first(fem.) — time — India — in?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: ji — yes. my(fem.) — health — very — bad — is.

lines.speaker: डॉक्टर:
lines.id: Don't worry. It happens to everyone.
lines.literal: panic — don't. this — all(obl.) — with — happens — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: How many days until I'm better?

lines.speaker: डॉक्टर:
lines.id: Two or three days. Take the medicine, rest, drink boiled water.
lines.literal: two-three — days. medicine — take, rest — do, boiled — water — drink.

notes: **Pain isn't owned; it's located somewhere.** *मेरे सिर **में** दर्द है* literally means "in my head there is pain". English says "my head hurts", making the head the subject; Hindi makes the **pain** the subject and the head the place. ⚠️ Note that मेरा becomes **मेरे** because में comes at the end — the oblique form from Unit 7 again.

**There are three ways to say it, all correct.** *मेरे सिर में दर्द है* (most common), *मुझे सिर में दर्द है* (with को, like Unit 8), *मेरा सिर दर्द कर रहा है* (literally "my head is making pain"). Use the first; recognize the other two when you hear them.

**कब से = since when, and से really does mean "since".** *कल से* (since yesterday), *दो दिन से* (for two days), *सुबह से* (since this morning). ⚠️ Note that Hindi uses the **present** for something still going on: *मैं दो दिन से बीमार **हूँ*** = "I've been ill for two days", literally "I am ill since two days". English uses "have been" here, so resist translating it word for word.

⚠️ **तबीयत — a word with a history.** It comes from Arabic *ṭabīʿa*, "nature, temperament" — but in Hindi-Urdu, **तबीयत means your state of health** — *मेरी तबीयत ख़राब है* = "I'm not feeling well", and *तबीयत कैसी है?* = "how are you feeling?". If you know the word from Arabic, Persian or Turkish, be ready for the shift.

⚠️ **तकलीफ़ has shifted too.** In Arabic, *taklīf* means a burden or an obligation. In Hindi, **तकलीफ़ means a complaint, trouble, discomfort** — and *क्या तकलीफ़ है?* is the first thing almost every doctor in India says. A related word that hasn't moved far: **आराम** (rest, comfort), from Persian, still means much the same as it always did.

**Health vocabulary is the biggest harvest from the Perso-Arabic layer.** सेहत (health), तबीयत, दवा, दवाख़ाना, मरीज़, इलाज, हकीम, बुख़ार, ज़ुकाम, तकलीफ़, आराम, आफ़ियत — nearly the whole Hindi health vocabulary comes from that one source. If you know any Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Turkish or Malay, this will be your easiest unit.

**घबराइए मत — and a set of reassuring phrases you'll hear all the time.** *घबराइए मत* (don't panic), *चिंता मत कीजिए* (don't worry), *सब ठीक हो जाएगा* (everything will be fine), *जल्दी ठीक हो जाइए* (get well soon). ⚠️ The last one is a natural wish to say to anyone who is ill, and in India it's said far more often than "get well soon" is in English.

grammars.title: The body and its complaints
after: ⚠️ **दिल means both the heart as an organ and the heart as the seat of feelings** — just like English "heart". *दिल का दर्द* can mean heart pain or heartbreak, and both are used. The word turns up in almost every film song ever written.

grammars.title: At the pharmacy and the hospital
after: ⚠️ In India, many medicines can be bought straight from a **मेडिकल स्टोर** without a prescription, and the pharmacist often gives advice. That's convenient, but for a fever that doesn't go down within two days, or a stomach upset with blood, **go to a doctor** — some mosquito-borne illnesses in India need a blood test, not guesswork.

sections.title: Looking after yourself, and asking after someone who's ill

blocks.text: An upset stomach in your first days in India is almost universal and has nothing to do with how clean the stall is — your stomach is just getting to know different germs. A few habits that really help:

items: **Drink sealed bottled water or boiled water.** Ask for **सील बंद बोतल** (*siil band bo-tal*) or **उबला पानी** (*ub-laa paa-nii*). It's best to skip the ice at small stalls during your first week.
**Hot food is safer than cold food.** Fritters and curries fresh from the pan are far safer than salads, peeled fruit, or sauces that have been sitting open.
**A busy stall is safer than a quiet one** — the ingredients turn over fast. Indians themselves always give this advice.
**Carry oral rehydration salts.** They're called **ओ आर एस** (*o aar es*), sold cheaply at every pharmacy, and work far faster than plain water.

⚠️ **Don't avoid street food forever.** Indian street food is among the best in the world, and skipping it altogether means missing much of what the country has to offer. Start slowly, choose what's hot and busy, and give your stomach a week.

blocks.title: Asking and answering about someone's health
items: **अब तबीयत कैसी है?** — How are you feeling now?
**अब कैसा लग रहा है?** — How do you feel now?
**पहले से बेहतर हूँ।** — Better than before.
**अभी भी ठीक नहीं।** — Still not well.
**दवा ली?** — Did you take your medicine?
**अपना ख़्याल रखिए।** — Take good care of yourself. ⚠️ A very warm goodbye, used far more widely than just when someone is ill.

blocks.text: One thing that may surprise you: if you fall ill in India and a local finds out — a neighbor, your host, a colleague — they'll very likely come over. Bringing food, asking how you are again and again, going to the doctor with you. Politely refusing that care is hard, and there's really no need to. Just say **आपका बहुत बहुत शुक्रिया** and accept it; in many parts of India, letting people look after you is how you show that you trust them.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

items: I've had a fever since last night.

answers: मेरे सिर में दर्द है। — क्या तकलीफ़ है? — कल रात से है। — चिंता मत कीजिए। — जल्दी ठीक हो जाइए।
मेरे सिर में दर्द है। — मुझे कल रात से बुख़ार है। — मेरी तबीयत ख़राब है। — बुख़ार की दवा दीजिए। — दिन में कितनी बार? — जल्दी ठीक हो जाइए।
